subject: physiology
title: Osmoreceptors, Thirst, Diabetes Insipidus, and SIADH

steps.tx: Homeostatic control of systemic extracellular fluid tonicity is mediated by exquisitely sensitive hypothalamic osmoreceptors located outside the blood-brain barrier. Situated within the **organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis** and subfornical organ, these specialized sensory neurons detect changes in extracellular fluid osmolality as small as one percent.
steps.say: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors in the lamina terminalis detect changes in plasma osmolality as small as one percent.

left.title: Hypothalamic Osmoreceptors
points: Located in OVLT and subfornical organ (circumventricular organs)
Lack blood-brain barrier; directly bathed by systemic arterial blood
Sensitive to effective osmoles (sodium, mannitol) that draw water
Insensitive to ineffective osmoles (urea, ethanol) that cross freely

right.title: Low-Pressure Baroreceptors
points: Located in cardiac atria and pulmonary great veins
Detect intravascular blood volume expansion or depletion
Less sensitive than osmoreceptors (requires 8% to 10% volume drop)
Potently stimulates vasopressin release during massive haemorrhage

steps.tx: When extracellular osmolality rises, water exits osmoreceptor neurons down its osmotic gradient, causing cellular dehydration and shrinkage. Mechanical deformation of stretch-inactivated cation channels depolarizes the membrane, driving axonal projection signals to the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei to trigger **vasopressin neurosecretion** into the systemic circulation.
steps.say: Hypertonicity shrinks osmoreceptors, opening cation channels that trigger vasopressin secretion and stimulate thirst.

nodes.label: Plasma Osmolality Rises Above 280 to 285 mOsm/kg Baseline
Osmotic Water Egress Causes Shrinkage of OVLT Osmoreceptor Neurons
Stretch-Inactivated Cation Channels Open, Eliciting Depolarization
Axonal Transport to Posterior Pituitary Releases Stored ADH / Vasopressin

steps.tx: Simultaneously, osmoreceptor activation projects to the limbic system and anterior cingulate cortex to stimulate the conscious **sensation of thirst**. The osmotic threshold for thirst is set approximately five milliosmoles higher than that for vasopressin release, ensuring that antidiuretic water retention acts as the first line of defense before drinking behavior is recruited.
steps.say: The thirst threshold is set five milliosmoles higher than vasopressin release, mobilizing drinking after antidiuresis begins.

rows: Preserves cardiac filling during severe shock

steps.tx: Failure of hypothalamic vasopressin synthesis or secretion produces **central diabetes insipidus**. Driven by idiopathic autoimmune destruction, pituitary surgery, or head trauma, the total absence of antidiuretic hormone prevents collecting duct water reabsorption, resulting in massive polyuria exceeding three to fifteen litres daily and unquenchable polydipsia.
steps.say: Central diabetes insipidus is the failure of vasopressin secretion, causing severe polyuria and thirst that responds to desmopressin.

left.title: Central Diabetes Insipidus
points: Deficient hypothalamic synthesis or posterior pituitary release
Caused by pituitary surgery, trauma, craniopharyngioma, histiocytosis
Urine osmolality < 300 mOsm/kg despite water deprivation
Exogenous desmopressin (dDAVP) increases urine osmolality by >50%

right.title: Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus
points: Normal or high circulating ADH; renal collecting duct resistance
Caused by V2 receptor mutations, lithium toxicity, hypercalcaemia
Urine osmolality remains < 300 mOsm/kg despite water deprivation
Exogenous desmopressin produces negligible change (<10% rise)

steps.tx: In contrast to central disease, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus arises from renal tubular unresponsiveness to circulating antidiuretic hormone despite normal or elevated plasma vasopressin levels. Chronic lithium therapy or hypercalcaemia impairs aquaporin-2 trafficking, rendering principal cells completely refractory to **exogenous desmopressin administration** during water deprivation testing.
steps.say: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus features kidney unresponsiveness to vasopressin, often triggered by lithium therapy or hypercalcaemia.

nodes.label: Standard Water Deprivation Test: Patient Deprived of Fluid for 8 Hours
Persistent Dilute Urine (Uosm < 300 mOsm/kg) with Rising Plasma Osmolality
Administer 1 to 2 mcg Subcutaneous Desmopressin (Synthetic V2 Agonist)
Central DI: Uosm Rises >50%; Nephrogenic DI: Uosm Fails to Rise (<10%)

steps.tx: Autonomous, unsuppressible oversecretion of vasopressin in the absence of osmotic or hemodynamic triggers constitutes the **syndrome of inappropriate ADH**. Ectopic secretion by small cell lung carcinoma, head trauma, or pulmonary infections causes excessive collecting duct water retention, producing progressive dilutional hyponatraemia.
steps.say: SIADH causes excessive water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia, commonly caused by lung cancer, CNS lesions, or drugs.

vis.alt: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone with water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia
vis.caption: Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone keeps water in, dilutes the plasma sodium, and is drawn with the usual triggers of lung cancer, brain disease and drugs. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Despite water retention, patients with SIADH present with **euvolaemic hyponatraemia** without peripheral edema. Expanding blood volume triggers atrial natriuretic peptide release, which enhances renal sodium excretion (natriuresis) while suppressing the renin-aldosterone axis, maintaining a normal extracellular fluid volume at the expense of severe plasma hypo-osmolality.
steps.say: SIADH presents as euvolaemic hyponatraemia because secondary natriuresis prevents edema while worsening hyponatremia.

rows: Dilutional hyponatraemia from excessive water retention
V2 activation prevents normal diluting capacity
ANP-induced secondary natriuresis prevents volume expansion
Absence of peripheral edema, ascites, or orthostatic hypotension

steps.tx: Sugar in the tubule drags water with it whether the kidney wishes or not. **Solute osmotic diuresis** happens when unreabsorbed glucose, mannitol or urea holds water in the lumen, producing large urine volumes with relatively fixed concentration. It is the mechanism behind polyuria in uncontrolled diabetes and behind some puzzling postoperative outputs. Measuring urine osmolality separates it from a pure water diuresis at the bedside laboratory.
steps.say: Unreabsorbed solute holds water in the tubule, causing osmotic diuresis in uncontrolled diabetes. Urine osmolality separates it from water diuresis.

vis.alt: Image showing solute osmotic diuresis with glucose holding water in the tubule lumen.
vis.caption: Glucose molecules in the lumen are shown dragging water toward the urine. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Differentiating high-volume urinary flow requires distinguishing water diuresis from **solute osmotic diuresis**. In water diuresis, urine osmolality is low and total solute excretion remains normal; in osmotic diuresis (such as diabetic ketoacidosis or mannitol infusion) high concentrations of unreabsorbed luminal solutes obligate immense water excretion alongside massive electrolyte wasting.
steps.say: Osmotic diuresis sheds unreabsorbed solutes like glucose or mannitol that drag water along, unlike pure water diuresis.

vis.alt: Renal electrolyte derangements and acute dialysis
vis.caption: Osmotic fluid loss, acute volume contraction, and renal replacement therapy in severe metabolic derangements.
